# This avoids HTML-specific function detection issues
make_table <- function(data, ...) {
  pandoc_to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
  if (!is.null(pandoc_to) && pandoc_to == "html") {
    return(kableExtra::kbl(data, ...))
  } else {
    return(knitr::kable(data, ...))
  }
}

op <- options(width = 120)
on.exit(options(op), add = TRUE)

`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) y else x

# Note: kable_styling and row_spec are HTML-specific and will cause errors in DOCX/PDF

# Find project root - use here() if available, otherwise try multiple strategies
if (requireNamespace("here", quietly = TRUE)) {
  proj_root <- here::here()
} else {
  # Strategy 1: Look for .git directory or README.md starting from current directory
  current_dir <- getwd()
  check_dir <- current_dir
  proj_root <- NULL
  
  for (i in 1:10) {  # Go up at most 10 levels
    if (file.exists(file.path(check_dir, ".git")) || 
        file.exists(file.path(check_dir, "README.md"))) {
      proj_root <- check_dir
      break
    }
    parent <- dirname(check_dir)
    if (parent == check_dir) break  # Reached filesystem root
    check_dir <- parent
  }
  
  # Strategy 2: If we're in reports/, go up 3 levels
  if (is.null(proj_root) && basename(current_dir) == "reports") {
    proj_root <- normalizePath(file.path(current_dir, "../../.."))
  }
  
  # Strategy 3: Default to current directory
  if (is.null(proj_root)) {
    proj_root <- current_dir
  }
}

# Helper: figure path resolution
# Returns PNG for HTML output, PDF for DOCX output
# Returns absolute path for file.exists() checks, relative path for include_graphics()
fig_path <- function(fig_name, return_absolute = FALSE) {
  # Get base name without extension
  base_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(fig_name)
  
  # Detect output format
  output_format <- NULL
  
  # Method 1: Check knitr's pandoc output format
  pandoc_to <- knitr::opts_knit$get("rmarkdown.pandoc.to")
  if (!is.null(pandoc_to)) {
    output_format <- pandoc_to
  }
  
  # Method 2: Check for DOCX rendering context
  if (is.null(output_format)) {
    docx_indicators <- c(
      knitr::opts_knit$get("quarto.document.format") == "docx",
      grepl("docx", knitr::opts_knit$get("out.format") %||% "", ignore.case = TRUE)
    )
    if (any(docx_indicators, na.rm = TRUE)) {
      output_format <- "docx"
    }
  }
  
  png_name <- paste0(base_name, ".png")
  pdf_name <- paste0(base_name, ".pdf")
  
  # Find the actual file location (use absolute paths for checking)
  png_abs <- NULL
  pdf_abs <- NULL
  
  # Try multiple candidate paths
  candidates_png <- c(
    file.path(figures_dir, png_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "06_visualization", "output", "figures", png_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "07_manuscript", "chapter2", "output", "figures", png_name),
    # Also try relative paths from current working directory
    file.path("../../../06_visualization/output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("../../06_visualization/output/figures", png_name),
    file.path("../06_visualization/output/figures", png_name)
  )
  
  candidates_pdf <- c(
    file.path(figures_dir, pdf_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "06_visualization", "output", "figures", pdf_name),
    file.path(proj_root, "07_manuscript", "chapter2", "output", "figures", pdf_name),
    # Also try relative paths from current working directory
    file.path("../../../06_visualization/output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("../../06_visualization/output/figures", pdf_name),
    file.path("../06_visualization/output/figures", pdf_name)
  )
  
  for (path in candidates_png) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      png_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  for (path in candidates_pdf) {
    if (file.exists(path)) {
      pdf_abs <- normalizePath(path)
      break
    }
  }
  
  # If return_absolute is TRUE, return absolute path (for file.exists checks)
  if (return_absolute) {
    if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      result <- pdf_abs %||% png_abs
    } else {
      result <- png_abs %||% pdf_abs
    }
    # Return NULL if no file found (file.exists(NULL) will return FALSE)
    return(result)
  }
  
  # Determine relative path based on current working directory
  # From reports/ to project root: reports -> chapter2 -> 07_manuscript -> root (3 levels up)
  # Then down to 06_visualization/output/figures
  if (basename(getwd()) == "reports" || grepl("/reports$", getwd())) {
    rel_path <- "../../../06_visualization/output/figures"
  } else {
    rel_path <- "06_visualization/output/figures"
  }
  
  # Return relative path for rendering
  if (!is.null(output_format) && grepl("docx|word", output_format, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
    if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, pdf_name))
    } else if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, png_name))
    }
  } else {
    # HTML: use relative path
    if (!is.null(png_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, png_name))
    } else if (!is.null(pdf_abs)) {
      return(file.path(rel_path, pdf_name))
    }
  }
  
  # Fallback
  warning("Figure not found: ", fig_name)
  return(file.path(rel_path, if (!is.null(png_abs)) png_name else pdf_name))
}

  }

    tryCatch(read_csv(path, show_col_types = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
  } else {
    NULL
  }
}

# Introduction

## Physical–Cognitive Dual-Task Interactions in Everyday Life and Aging

Everyday life frequently requires people to perform cognitively demanding tasks while simultaneously exerting physical effort. Surgeons must maintain continuous muscle engagement while making fine perceptual discriminations, athletes coordinate complex motor sequences while monitoring environmental cues, and older adults navigate dual-task situations—such as walking while monitoring traffic or carrying groceries while having a conversation—in which physical and cognitive demands interact dynamically. These real-world scenarios highlight a fundamental challenge: when multiple task domains compete for limited cognitive resources, performance in one or both domains may suffer [@wickens2008; @pashler1994dual]. This challenge takes on particular significance in aging, as older adults face both declining cognitive capacity and increased physiological costs of effortful engagement [@salthouse1996; @verhaeghen2003].

A growing literature suggests that physical–cognitive interactions are mediated by shared arousal systems, particularly the locus coeruleus–noradrenergic (LC–NE) system, which modulates sensory gain, evidence accumulation, and response caution as a function of task demands and internal state [@astonjones2005; @mather2016; @jepma2012neural]. Understanding how physical effort modulates cognitive performance—and how this relationship changes with age—requires moving beyond simple outcome measures (overall accuracy or mean reaction time) to characterize how effort-induced arousal alters the fundamental processes underlying perceptual decision-making. The present study addresses this question by combining a physical–cognitive dual-task paradigm with pupillometry and psychometric function analysis to examine how physical effort–induced arousal relates to perceptual sensitivity in older adults.

## Psychometric Functions: Quantifying Perceptual Sensitivity

Psychometric functions (PFs) provide a principled framework for characterizing how continuous stimulus intensity relates to perceptual judgments. Rather than collapsing performance across stimulus levels, PFs model the full intensity–response relationship, revealing how the probability of a given response changes as stimulus differences become more or less discriminable. In the present same–different discrimination paradigm, the PF maps a continuous intensity dimension (e.g., frequency offset or contrast difference) onto the probability of responding "different" [@wichmann2001psychometric; @green1966signal; @prins2016psychophysics]. This perspective aligns with a measurement-model view of perception: PFs can be derived from latent sensory evidence that is corrupted by internal noise and then transformed into an overt response via a decision rule [@prins2016psychophysics]. Within this framework, changes in PF steepness are typically interpreted as changes in discriminability (signal-to-noise separation), whereas horizontal shifts can reflect changes in response tendency or criterion, and thus require more cautious interpretation when the task permits bias [@macmillan2005detection].

Psychometric functions take sigmoidal (S-shaped) forms and can be expressed using several closely related link families, including the cumulative normal (probit), logistic (logit), and Weibull functions. For a binary response model, one common formulation is the probit PF:

$$P(\text{"different"} | X) = \Phi\left(\frac{X - \alpha}{\beta}\right)$$ {#eq-psychometric}

where $X$ denotes stimulus intensity, $\Phi(\cdot)$ is the cumulative standard normal distribution, $\alpha$ is a location parameter corresponding to the stimulus intensity at which responding reaches a criterion level (often defined at a midpoint between asymptotes), and $\beta$ is a scale/spread parameter. Under this parameterization, PF steepness is inversely related to $\beta$: smaller $\beta$ values yield steeper functions (higher discriminability), whereas larger $\beta$ values yield shallower functions (lower discriminability). The steepness directly reflects discriminability—how rapidly the probability of choosing "different" changes as stimulus intensity increases. Under the probit parameterization, the standard deviation of the underlying sensory noise distribution is $\sigma = \beta$ (the scale parameter directly corresponds to the noise SD). An analogous logit specification replaces $\Phi(\cdot)$ with the logistic function, and in practice different sigmoid families typically yield very similar fits, with differences primarily reflecting parameterization and threshold conventions [@prins2016psychophysics]. For example, the Weibull's conventional threshold parameter corresponds to approximately 0.632 on the cumulative response scale, whereas Quick/log-Quick formulations correspond to 0.5; therefore, threshold values should always be interpreted relative to the criterion at which they are defined [@prins2016psychophysics].

In many psychophysical applications, PFs include asymptotes: a guess rate ($\gamma$) and a lapse rate ($\lambda$) that capture stimulus-independent errors; assuming $\lambda=0$ when lapses are present can bias threshold and slope estimates [@prins2016psychophysics; @wichmann2001psychometric]. The four-parameter formulation is:

$$P(\text{"different"} | X) = \gamma + (1 - \gamma - \lambda) \cdot \Phi\left(\frac{X - \alpha}{\beta}\right)$$

**Location** ($\alpha$) and **steepness** (inverse of scale) must be distinguished: in same–different tasks, shifts in $\alpha$ can reflect criterion/bias as well as sensitivity, whereas steepness indexes how rapidly response probability changes with intensity and is the cleaner sensitivity index [@prins2016psychophysics; @macmillan2005detection]. This contrast is illustrated in @fig-pf-location-vs-sensitivity.

These considerations connect directly to signal detection theory: location shifts can reflect criterion changes (response bias), while changes in steepness reflect true sensitivity changes [@macmillan2005detection]. In the present same–different judgment task, the GLMM includes random intercepts to absorb individual differences in response criterion, while the intensity × pupil-state interaction term targets sensitivity (steepness) rather than bias.

This chapter leverages two complementary PF approaches that serve distinct purposes. First, descriptive PF parameters (thresholds and slopes) that provide the behavioral backbone for Chapter 2 were estimated previously using Psignifit 4 in MATLAB [@schutt2016painfree], which supports robust estimation and can account for overdispersion. A Weibull PF was fit to each participant's proportion of "different" responses across stimulus levels within each task and effort condition. Because the Weibull function is undefined at zero, **0-offset** trials (physically identical standard and probe) were assigned intensities of **4 Hz** (**ADT**) and **0.0075** Michelson contrast (**VDT**)—each **half of the smallest non-zero stimulus level** in that modality—preserving the full difficulty ladder while satisfying the fitting engine. Guess and lapse parameters were allowed to vary freely during fitting, and threshold and slope were derived at the effective midpoint—halfway between the estimated guess rate $\gamma$ and $1-\lambda$—yielding a criterion comparable to a 50% point on the effective response scale.

Second, the primary inferential analyses in the present chapter use a hierarchical generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with a probit link to model trialwise $P(\text{"different"} \mid X)$. In a probit-link GLMM, the linear predictor operates on a latent standard-normal ($z$) evidence scale, and the intensity coefficient governs the steepness of the intensity–response relationship in that latent space. The critical interaction between stimulus intensity and within-person pupil state ($X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$) therefore tests whether moment-to-moment arousal modulates sensitivity (steepness) rather than merely shifting response tendency (criterion). Although the trial-level GLMM does not explicitly estimate lapse parameters, lapse-like contamination is minimized through stringent pupil quality tiers and robustness checks, preserving statistical efficiency while addressing psychophysical concerns about stimulus-independent error. The probit link function is used in the GLMM for consistency with the latent evidence interpretation in signal detection theory, where the cumulative normal distribution naturally maps onto $z$-scaled evidence. In the present study, stimulus intensity is modeled on its original scale (frequency offset in Hz for auditory, contrast difference for visual), and the continuous-intensity GLMM framework avoids binning regardless of the underlying scale—preserving information and statistical efficiency relative to collapsing trials into coarse difficulty bins. Continuous modeling preserves the full intensity–response relationship and tests whether arousal alters the rate of evidence accumulation (sensitivity), not only response tendency.

## Arousal, Effort, and Perceptual Sensitivity

The relationship between arousal and cognitive performance has been formalized in several influential frameworks. The Yerkes–Dodson law proposes an inverted-U function in which performance improves with increasing arousal up to an optimal point, beyond which additional arousal—particularly when experienced as stress or anxiety—impairs performance [@yerkes1908]. Adaptive Gain Theory (AGT) provides a mechanistic account centered on the locus coeruleus–norepinephrine (LC–NE) system, linking tonic (baseline) and phasic (event-evoked) LC activity to shifts in neural gain and, ultimately, task performance [@astonjones2005]. Under AGT, optimal performance is expected when tonic LC activity is moderate and phasic responses to task-relevant events are robust, supporting focused attention and efficient responding.

In aging, arousal–performance relationships may be altered in ways that complicate these canonical predictions. Evidence suggests that older adults may exhibit a leftward shift or compression of the inverted-U curve, such that peak performance occurs at lower levels of objective demand relative to younger adults [@mather2016; @mikneviciute2022]. As a result, conditions that are neutral or even beneficial for younger adults may push older adults into supra-optimal arousal states, placing them on the descending limb of the curve and producing performance decrements [@huang2024; @mather2016]. This aging-related vulnerability motivates testing whether experimentally induced arousal—here, physical effort—selectively disrupts the quality of perceptual evidence and the sensitivity of discrimination.

Physical effort provides a controlled method for manipulating arousal state in a way that is experimentally separable from stimulus difficulty. Sustained isometric handgrip at moderate-to-high intensities (e.g., ~30–40% MVC) elicits a robust pressor and sympathoexcitatory response—raising arterial pressure and heart rate and increasing sympathetic outflow—whose magnitude scales with contraction intensity and remains present in older adults. At the neural level, static handgrip and post-exercise ischemia recruit brainstem and cortical regions involved in autonomic control and effort, offering a plausible central substrate for effort-induced arousal shifts that may interact with perceptual decision processes [@lalande2014; @mark1985; @sander2010; @toska2010]. This provides an experimentally useful perturbation of arousal-related physiology, but it should not be treated as isomorphic with tonic LC firing: handgrip-induced sympathoexcitation is only an indirect route into the LC-linked mechanisms emphasized by AGT.

At the same time, physical effort may influence performance through mechanisms that are not purely "arousal," including resource-based interference. Limited-capacity and multiple-resource accounts predict that concurrent physical effort can compete with cognitive task performance when total demands exceed available capacity or when tasks draw on overlapping resource pools [@wickens2008]. Supporting this possibility, Azer et al. [-@azer2023] reported that older adults showed reduced accuracy in a visual working memory task while maintaining moderate handgrip (30% MVC), whereas younger adults were relatively unaffected. This pattern is consistent with the idea that older adults may be more susceptible to combined physical-cognitive demands, either because resources are depleted more readily or because arousal becomes dysregulated under challenge [@verhaeghen2003]. Importantly, these "resource competition" and "arousal regulation" perspectives are not mutually exclusive, and the present study is designed to adjudicate between them by modeling trialwise arousal (pupil state) alongside effort condition.

These frameworks motivate specific predictions for psychometric sensitivity. Location (midpoint) shifts can reflect criterion/bias in same–different tasks and are interpreted cautiously (see @fig-pf-location-vs-sensitivity); steepness provides the primary index of discriminability. If effort-induced arousal degrades signal quality or increases noise, functions should become shallower; moderate arousal could steepen them. Supra-optimal arousal may be more likely in older adults, motivating emphasis on steepness and its modulation by pupil-indexed arousal rather than on threshold alone.

## Pupillometry as a Window into Arousal Dynamics

The LC–NE system is a central regulator of arousal and cognitive state. As the primary source of norepinephrine to the forebrain, LC–NE projections modulate neural gain and the signal-to-noise ratio of cortical processing [@astonjones2005]. AGT posits that task performance depends on a balance between tonic LC activity and phasic LC bursts, such that moderate tonic baseline paired with strong phasic responses supports focused attention and effective behavioral control [@gilzenrat2010].

Pupillometry provides a practical, noninvasive index of arousal dynamics that is often linked to LC–NE activity. Pupil diameter covaries with arousal-related neuromodulatory activity and can be characterized at two levels. First, baseline (tonic) pupil diameter reflects relatively sustained arousal state and has been associated with tonic LC activity and general alertness [@alnaes2014pupil; @gilzenrat2010]. Second, task-evoked pupil responses (TEPRs) reflect event-linked changes often interpreted as phasic arousal and mobilization of mental effort during task execution [@beatty1982; @kahneman1966]. TEPRs typically peak on the order of 1–2 seconds after stimulus onset and can be quantified using peak amplitude, mean dilation over a defined epoch, or the area under the curve (AUC) of the baseline-corrected signal, which jointly captures amplitude and duration. TEPR magnitude has been linked to task difficulty, cognitive load, surprise, and decision confidence, and in discrimination contexts larger TEPRs often accompany more difficult decisions, consistent with increased recruitment of control resources [@kiefer2018; @preuschoff2011pupil]. The neural pathway linking LC to pupil diameter involves direct projections from LC to the Edinger–Westphal nucleus, which controls pupil constriction/dilation via parasympathetic and sympathetic pathways [@joshi2016; @mcDougal2010; @murphy2014].

Interpretation of pupil diameter nevertheless requires care because pupillometry is a multi-determined signal shaped by interacting neural and autonomic pathways. While LC–NE contributions to pupil fluctuations are central to the present theoretical framing, other structures and pathways can also influence pupil dynamics, and measurement artifacts can distort pupil estimates [@papesh2024modern]. In particular, eye position and saccade-related effects can alter apparent pupil size (e.g., pupil foreshortening error and post-saccadic pupil constrictions), and blink-related missingness can bias mean or baseline estimates if not handled carefully [@laeng2024; @hershman2024]. In cognitive tasks, TEPRs reflect event-linked changes that unfold with a physiological delay rather than instantaneously; pupil changes are typically detectable approximately 200–250 ms after task events, with responses tied to specific events such as stimulus presentation, response execution, or feedback [@hershman2024]. This temporal delay justifies the use of epoch-based analysis windows and AUC metrics that capture the full time course of the response. These considerations motivate pairing theory-driven pupil metrics with explicit preprocessing and data-quality procedures designed to minimize artifactual variance and ensure that observed effects reflect task-evoked physiology rather than measurement confounds. In the present chapter, that means the primary GLMM should be interpreted as a test of **phasic**, stimulus-locked pupil coupling with psychometric sensitivity; tonic pupil state is addressed only indirectly via the effort manipulation checks.

In aging, LC–NE regulation may change in ways that are directly relevant to arousal–performance coupling. Structural degradation of the LC has been observed in older adults [@mather2016], and functional compensatory patterns may emerge, including chronically elevated tonic arousal or altered phasic responsiveness to challenge [@lee2018; @mather2016neural]. Such compensatory dynamics may support performance up to a point, but could also increase vulnerability to supra-optimal arousal, leading to distractibility and degraded information processing under high demand [@astonjones2005; @eldar2013]. Pupillometry studies in aging report heterogeneous patterns—often larger baseline pupils coupled with reduced task-evoked responses—suggesting altered tonic-phasic balance [@granholm2007]. Physical effort manipulations therefore provide an opportunity to test whether externally induced arousal shifts pupil dynamics and whether trialwise pupil state predicts changes in psychometric sensitivity.

## Dual-Task Context and Competing Mechanisms

Dual-task paradigms have long been used to understand limits of attention and performance under concurrent demands. Limited-capacity and resource-competition accounts propose that performance decrements arise when combined task demands exceed available resources, particularly when tasks draw on overlapping pools of attention or executive control [@kahneman1973; @navon1984; @navon1985; @wickens2008]. Multiple Resource Theory further predicts that interference depends on similarity across resource dimensions (e.g., spatial vs. verbal demands), such that tasks that share processing channels are more likely to interfere [@wickens2008]. Applied to physical–cognitive dual tasks, interference may arise through sustained attentional requirements for maintaining force, physiological arousal effects that can help or harm performance depending on state, and motor–cognitive competition that affects response selection and execution [@proctor2012; @woollacott2002]. Age-related increases in dual-task costs are well documented and may reflect reduced reserve, altered executive control, or changes in arousal regulation [@beurskens2014; @verhaeghen2003].

The present study explicitly recognizes that effort effects may reflect both generic resource competition and arousal-mediated mechanisms. Resource-competition models predict effort-related performance decrements as demands rise, whereas arousal-based accounts (including LC–NE mechanisms) predict that the quality of information processing may change as a function of arousal state, potentially independent of capacity limits. The key advantage of pairing pupillometry with psychometric modeling is that it allows these mechanisms to be separated empirically: effort condition provides an experimental manipulation, while trialwise pupil state indexes moment-to-moment arousal, and the psychometric framework distinguishes sensitivity changes (steepness) from criterion shifts (intercept/location). Accordingly, effort main effects in the GLMM may reflect a mixture of resource and arousal influences, whereas a significant stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction would more specifically support arousal-linked modulation of sensitivity.

## Linking Arousal to Psychometric Sensitivity: Analytic Strategy

A central methodological challenge in pupil–behavior analyses is separating within-person "state" fluctuations from between-person "trait" differences. To do so, each pupil metric ($P_{ij}$) is decomposed into a subject-mean component and a trial-wise deviation using within-subject centering:

$$P^{(\text{trait})}_{j} = \overline{P}_{j}, \qquad P^{(\text{state})}_{ij} = P_{ij} - \overline{P}_{j}$$ {#eq-state-trait}

This decomposition enables two distinct questions to be tested in the same model: whether individuals with higher average arousal differ in sensitivity (trait effects), and whether trials on which an individual is more aroused than usual show altered sensitivity (state effects). Importantly, this approach prevents conflating between- and within-person patterns—an especially relevant concern in aging where trait differences may be influenced by health or cognitive reserve [@enders2013; @hoffman2015]. For example, if high-arousal individuals tend to have poorer performance for reasons unrelated to trial-wise fluctuations (e.g., chronic health conditions or comorbidities), that pattern will be captured at the trait level rather than falsely attributed to trial-wise changes in arousal. @fig-decompose-state-trait illustrates this decomposition visually, showing how raw pupil metrics are separated into trait (between-person) and state (within-person) components.

```{r decompose-state-trait}
#| label: fig-decompose-state-trait
#| fig-cap: >
#|   **Integrated schematic: within-subject arousal and psychometric sensitivity.**
#|   **(A)** Raw pupil problem. Baseline pupil diameter differs between people, so the same raw value can mean high arousal for one participant and low arousal for another; raw values are therefore misleading for cross-person comparisons.
#|   **(B)** Trait versus state decomposition. Each trial-level pupil metric $P_{ij}$ splits into a **trait** component, the subject mean $\overline{P}_j$, and a **state** component, the deviation from that mean, $P_{ij} - \overline{P}_j = P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$.
#|   **(C)** Inferential goal: slope modulation. The primary interaction ($X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$) tests whether moment-to-moment arousal changes the steepness (sensitivity) of the psychometric function, not only intercept or criterion.
#|   **(D)** Measurement window and model. The timeline shows squeeze onset through trial end; the shaded **Cognitive AUC** window (4.85--6.05 s from squeeze onset) captures task-evoked pupil response. The equation summarizes the probit-link GLMM used for inference (full specification in text).
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "100%"

if (file.exists(decompose_fig_path)) {

} else {

```

Primary inference is implemented using hierarchical generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) with a probit link, modeling trialwise $P(Y_{ij}=1)$ as a function of continuous stimulus intensity, effort condition, modality, and pupil-indexed arousal while accounting for individual differences via random effects:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{probit}(P(Y_{ij}=1)) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Effort}_{ij} + \beta_3 \text{Modality}_{ij} + \beta_4 P^{(\text{state})}_{ij} \\
&\quad + \beta_5 (X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}) + \beta_6 P^{(\text{trait})}_{j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j}X_{ij}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-primary-glmm}

where $Y_{ij}$ is the binary outcome on trial $i$ for subject $j$, $X_{ij}$ is the continuous stimulus intensity, $\text{Effort}_{ij}$ codes the handgrip effort condition (High vs. Low), and $\text{Modality}_{ij}$ codes the sensory modality (auditory vs. visual). $P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$ and $P^{(\text{trait})}_{j}$ are the state and trait components of the pupil metric, respectively, and $u_{0j}$ and $u_{1j}$ are subject-specific random intercepts and random slopes on $X_{ij}$, allowing each participant to have their own baseline performance level and intensity sensitivity. The full specification is given in @sec-glmm.

In this framework, the key parameter is the stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction ($\beta_5$), which tests whether moment-to-moment arousal modulates psychometric sensitivity. A significant interaction indicates that the intensity–response slope differs as a function of trialwise arousal—consistent with arousal-linked changes in sensitivity—whereas changes limited to intercept/location terms would be more consistent with shifts in response tendency or criterion.

## Research Questions and Hypotheses

Based on the theoretical rationale above, the present study addresses four research questions. First, we test how high (40% MVC) versus low (5% MVC) effort affects behavioral psychometric function parameters (thresholds and slopes) in older adults performing auditory and visual same–different discrimination. We expect midpoint thresholds to be higher under high effort, acknowledging that threshold shifts may reflect sensitivity and/or criterion changes, and we predict shallower slopes under high effort, consistent with reduced discriminability under elevated arousal.

Second, we test whether high effort increases tonic and task-evoked pupil dynamics relative to low effort. We predict larger baseline pupil diameter and larger TEPR (AUC) under high effort, indicating elevated tonic and phasic arousal, respectively.

Third, we test whether trialwise phasic arousal predicts psychometric sensitivity when intensity is modeled continuously. The primary hypothesis is that the stimulus intensity × pupil-state interaction will be negative (shallower slopes on higher-arousal trials), consistent with supra-optimal arousal increasing noise or degrading signal quality; an alternative hypothesis is that moderate arousal could enhance sensitivity, yielding a positive interaction. We also expect weaker or null associations for pupil-trait predictors, given that trait effects may be confounded with other individual differences such as cognitive reserve.

Finally, we test whether individuals with larger effort-evoked arousal changes (Δpupil) exhibit larger effort-related changes in psychometric parameters (Δthreshold, Δslope), predicting that stronger physiological reactivity is associated with larger behavioral decrements.

# Methods

<!-- Add your methods section here -->

## Participants

Older adults (*M* = 69.1 years, *SD* = 6.0, range 60--83; 33 women, 28 men) were enrolled through the LC Aging study behavioral cohort (community-dwelling volunteers enrolled for combined behavioral and neuroimaging protocols). Task-specific recruitment and final analytic sample sizes are summarized in @tbl-sample-flow (Section 3.1): **64** participants were recruited for the **auditory** task (ADT) and **65** for the **visual** task (VDT), with **54** and **56** participants, respectively, retained for the pupil-QC final sample after psychometric and pupil-quality exclusions ([@sec-sample-retention](#sec-sample-retention)). **Sixty-one** unique participants contributed overlapping trial-level data to the merged behavioral--pupil file. Consistent with the final per-task analytic *N* in @tbl-sample-flow (**54** ADT; **56** VDT), **49** participants met inclusion criteria for **both** modalities, **5** for **ADT** only, and **7** for **VDT** only. Reported years of formal education averaged 15.9 (*SD* = 2.6; *n* = 57 with non-missing values in the study database). Participants with trial-level data in the present analysis were right-handed per eligibility records. Participants were included if they were aged 60 years or older, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, reported no significant hearing loss that would preclude tone discrimination, and were free of neurological, psychiatric, or cardiovascular conditions that could affect arousal regulation or pupil dynamics. Participants taking medications known to affect pupil diameter (e.g., anticholinergics, opioids, alpha-adrenergic agents) were excluded, as were individuals who could not safely sustain the required isometric grip forces (5% and 40% maximum voluntary contraction [MVC]) or had other contraindications to the effort manipulation. Cognitive screening used the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) administered by phone (scored out of 22); among participants with scores in the research database (*n* = 57), MoCA ranged from 17 to 22 (*M* = 19.8, *SD* = 1.6), consistent with study criteria for excluding significant cognitive impairment. All participants provided written informed consent. The research protocol was reviewed and approved by an institutional review board before enrollment, and participants received compensation for their participation according to study policy.

Trial-level analyses use the merged behavioral--pupil file. **Quality-primary** trial counts and participant-flow accounting are reported in Section 3.1 (@tbl-sample-flow); the primary GLMM uses the complete-case subset with non-missing cognitive pupil state, stimulus intensity, and choice (@sec-power-analysis).

## Task Paradigm

**Task overview.** Participants completed two **same–different discrimination** tasks—an Auditory Discrimination Task (ADT) and a Visual Discrimination Task (VDT)—while maintaining concurrent isometric hand-grip on a dynamometer. On each trial, a *standard* and *probe* stimulus were presented in sequence; participants judged whether the two were the same or different, then rated their confidence. Both tasks used the same response-signal timeline and effort manipulation (@fig-paradigm).

**Trial timeline and effort.** Each trial began with a **jittered** blank interval (1.5–4.5 s) on a gray background. Participants then saw a **3 s** rectangular grip gauge whose marker indicated the target force—either **5%** or **40%** of maximum voluntary contraction (MVC)—to be held with the left hand on a handheld dynamometer. MVC was assessed in a short calibration before each task. Participants were instructed to maintain force near the marker until the response screens appeared (see schematic). After the grip period came a **0.25 s** blank, a **0.5 s** fixation dot, the two-stimulus sequence (standard → **0.5 s** ISI → probe), a **0.25 s** blank, a **3 s** same/different response window, and a **3 s** four-point confidence rating. From **squeeze onset** through the end of the confidence period, the fixed portion of the timeline lasted **10.7 s**; including the pre-trial jitter and the preprocessed pre-squeeze baseline used for pupil segmentation, the full trial epoch matches the **13.7 s** timeline used in the MATLAB preprocessing pipeline.

Auditory and visual stimulus classes are summarized in the task sections below; timing follows the schematic.
#| fig-width: 10

**Auditory task (ADT).** The standard was a **0.1 s** sinusoidal tone at **1000 Hz**. After a **0.5 s** ISI, the probe was a **0.1 s** tone identical to the standard (**Δfrequency** = 0) or frequency-incremented by **8, 16, 32, or 64 Hz**.

**Visual task (VDT).** The standard was a foveal sinusoidal Gabor patch (**1.5** cycles/°, Michelson contrast **0.20**, diameter **4°**, duration **0.1 s**). The probe matched the standard (**Δcontrast** = 0) or increased in contrast by **0.06, 0.12, 0.24, or 0.48** with other parameters fixed.

**Responses.** After stimulus offset, participants released the grip and used the **right** hand to respond within **3 s** (index finger = “different,” middle finger = “same”). A **3 s** confidence screen followed (four levels, 1 = lowest to 4 = highest confidence).

**Scheduling and feedback.** Each task comprised **150** trials per full set (**five** blocks of **30**), crossing the five stimulus levels (standard plus four offsets) with the two effort conditions in pseudorandom order with equal allocation (three trials per stimulus × effort combination per block when the full schedule was collected). Grip performance was reviewed between blocks; participants received corrective feedback if force was repeatedly off-target or not maintained through the probe as required. Task runs were acquired in-scanner (**Session 2** and **Session 3** in the study database; practice and Session 1 were excluded from analysis files). Low- and high-effort trials were **intermixed within runs** rather than blocked by session. Realized trial counts vary when runs were omitted (Section 3.1).

Stimuli were presented and responses collected using the LC Aging in-scanner setup: visual stimulation via a PROPixx-class projector (VPixx Technologies; high refresh rate, HD resolution) viewed through a head-coil mirror at approximately **12 cm** effective viewing distance; auditory stimulation through MRI-compatible earphones; fiber-optic response hardware for choices; MRI-compatible dynamometer for grip force; and binocular eye tracking for pupil diameter (**250 Hz** in the processed data used here; see Pupillometry). Stimulus delivery and timing used Psychophysics Toolbox in MATLAB; neuroimaging results are reported elsewhere.

## Pupillometry

Pupil diameter was recorded continuously throughout each trial at **250 Hz** and processed using a MATLAB preprocessing pipeline that segments trials relative to squeeze onset, flags blinks and track loss events, computes window-specific validity metrics, and implements subtractive baseline correction using pre-event windows.

**Metrics and preprocessing.** The first derived measure was **Total AUC**: baseline-corrected area under the pupil curve over a global trial window, indexing overall arousal during concurrent physical effort. The second, which served as the primary predictor in trial-level models, was the **cognitive pupil metric**: a baseline-corrected, task-evoked summary from a fixed **1.20 s** stimulus-locked window spanning 4.85--6.05 s (target onset + 0.50 s through +1.70 s relative to squeeze onset). That window targets the task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) peak, which typically occurs about one second after stimulus onset [@mathot2023methods], while limiting early reflex contributions and RT-driven confounds. Analyses used **mean dilation** (AUC divided by window duration) rather than raw AUC, which removes duration confounds and is the preferred summary for this window. The distribution of Cognitive AUC was checked against a physiological-ceiling interpretation; results of that check are reported in Section 3.3 with the effort–pupil manipulation.

Baseline correction was implemented subtractively (*pupil* - baseline mean). For **Total AUC**, the baseline window was the pre-squeeze interval from **−0.5 s to 0.0 s** relative to squeeze onset (B0 baseline). For the **cognitive pupil metric**, the baseline window was the pre-target interval from **3.85 s to 4.35 s** relative to squeeze onset (B1 baseline). This target-proximal baseline was chosen so that the cognitive window reflects event-linked dilation relative to the immediately preceding pre-target pupil level, while the global Total AUC reflects overall dilation across the sustained effort epoch.

**Quality control and confound mitigation.** Gap-aware quality control metrics were developed following @kret2019preprocessing to distinguish genuine low pupil dilation from data quality artifacts arising from fragmented missing-data segments. A trial can have acceptable overall validity (e.g., 60%) yet contain a large contiguous gap that distorts AUC estimates; percentage-validity thresholds are therefore not always sufficient for quality screening. Full metric specifications are given in [Appendix A](#sec-appendix-a), but the saved model objects reported in this chapter were fit using the processed dataset's `quality_primary`, `quality_lenient`, and `quality_strict` flags.

Pupil-based analyses used three pre-defined percentage-validity tiers from the processed dataset. The **primary** tier required `baseline_quality >= 0.60` and `cog_quality >= 0.60`; the **lenient** tier used thresholds of 0.50 for both; the **strict** tier required 0.70 for both. An expanded B1/gap-aware screening framework was developed in parallel preprocessing documentation, but those thresholds were not the operative inclusion flags for the saved analysis objects summarized here. Accordingly, the reported results should be interpreted as reflecting the simpler percentage-validity tiers above.

Psychophysical modeling guidance emphasizes that **assuming lapse rate ($\lambda$) = 0 can distort threshold and slope estimates** if lapses are present but unaccounted for [@prins2016psychophysics]. This concern is particularly relevant in older adult populations, where attentional lapses, track loss events, and data quality issues may be more frequent. The quality-tier strategy addresses this by excluding trials with poorer pupil validity, thereby reducing lapse-like contamination in the psychometric function estimates. The tiering approach tests robustness of conclusions across stricter inclusion criteria: if key effects (e.g., the stimulus intensity × pupil state interaction) are consistent across lenient, primary, and strict quality tiers, this provides evidence that findings are not driven solely by the specific validity threshold used. This strategy is consistent with psychophysical best practices for handling stimulus-independent errors without explicitly estimating lapse parameters in the primary model [@prins2016psychophysics].

### Cognitive window and response-screen timing {#sec-response-timing}

The cognitive AUC window unavoidably overlaps task events that can contaminate pupil measurements: the target appears at 4.35 s (relative to squeeze onset), the response screen at 4.70 s (350 ms after target), and the button press at a variable time. In the primary GLMM sample, **RT** was measured from response-screen onset (4.70 s); median RT was `r if (!is.null(response_timing)) format_rt_s(response_timing$median_rt) else "—"` s overall (`r format_task_timing(response_timing, "median_rt")`), corresponding to median press times of `r if (!is.null(response_timing)) format_rt_s(response_timing$median_press) else "—"` s relative to squeeze onset (`r format_task_timing(response_timing, "median_press")`). These values align with the median response markers in @fig-pupil-timeseries. The analytic goal is not to eliminate these confounds—which is impossible—but to limit their impact, acknowledge what remains, and support conclusions with sensitivity analyses.

Accordingly, the primary cognitive window (4.85--6.05 s) was **stimulus-locked and of fixed duration**, and the pupil summary was **mean dilation** (AUC divided by duration), which together reduce mechanical coupling of RT to AUC and duration-related artifacts relative to raw AUC. Motor-buffered and pre-response window definitions were also pre-computed (truncating the primary window 150 ms before button press, and a decision-aligned window excluding the final 150 ms before response, respectively); full AUC computation for those windows requires re-processing and is reserved for future sensitivity analyses ([Appendix E](#sec-appendix-e)). Finally, a **slow-RT** sensitivity subset flags trials where the button press falls after the cognitive window (RT > 1.5 s, press after 6.20 s), so motor execution cannot overlap the pupil epoch; that subset feeds the analysis in Section 3.5.1 and [Appendix B](#sec-appendix-b).

### Sample retention and exclusions by task {#sec-sample-retention}

Participant flow was evaluated **separately by modality** because psychometric validity and pupil-data quality were gated independently for ADT and VDT (@sec-analytic-samples). Of **64** participants recruited for the **auditory** task, **54** entered the **pupil-QC final sample** (**10** excluded from that stream). Of those **10**, **3** had **Psignifit** **thresholds** above **64 Hz** (prespecified PF invalidity) and **7** had **excessive eye-track loss** (greater than **50%** invalid samples) or other **pupil QC failures**. For PF inference, only the three ADT threshold-invalid participants are excluded from the PF-valid sample (**61** ADT with converged, in-range fits); pupil-QC failure does not exclude participants from PF analyses. Of **65** participants recruited for the **visual** task, **56** entered the **pupil-QC final sample** (**9** excluded). **None** of the **visual** exclusions were attributed to PF **threshold** estimates; **all nine** reflected **track loss** or **QC failures**. These counts align with @tbl-sample-flow (Section 3.1).

## Statistical Analysis

### Analytic sample streams {#sec-analytic-samples}

**Pupil-quality exclusions** gate trial-level GLMM analyses, effort–pupil manipulation checks, and missingness diagnostics. **PF-validity exclusions** gate descriptive and inferential psychometric-function analyses: converged fits only, and for ADT, threshold estimates at or below the maximum tested offset (64 Hz). Pupil-QC failure has no bearing on behavioral PF inference; conversely, PF-invalid fits are excluded from PF summaries regardless of pupil data quality. The two streams therefore differ in *N* by design (@tbl-sample-flow). Within the pupil-QC stream, the primary GLMM further requires complete cognitive pupil metrics and choice data, so its trial count is smaller than the quality-primary gate alone (Section 3.1). Subject-level PF–pupil coupling uses the intersection of both streams (valid PF change scores and primary-tier pupil data in both effort conditions), which is why coupling *N* is smaller than either stream alone.

**Psychometric function fitting.** Behavioral data were fit in **Psignifit 4** (MATLAB; @schutt2016painfree) using a **beta-binomial** observation model for the counts of "different" responses at each stimulus level. This choice was motivated by **overdispersion**: at a given intensity, empirical variability in binary outcomes can exceed the variance implied by a standard binomial model, which assumes independent Bernoulli trials with a single underlying probability. The beta-binomial formulation relaxes that assumption by introducing a **dispersion metric** $\eta$ (eta), estimated jointly with the psychometric function parameters. Together with threshold and slope (and asymptotic parameters), $\eta$ indexes extra-binomial variability and supports more robust parameter recovery when performance fluctuates beyond simple binomial sampling error.

Psychometric function parameters (thresholds and slopes) used as the behavioral backbone were taken from these fits. A **Weibull psychometric function** was fit to the proportion of "different" responses across continuous stimulus intensity levels, separately for each participant × task/modality × effort condition.

**Zero-intensity replacement (Weibull compatibility).** The **Weibull** link is **undefined** at a stimulus intensity of **0**. Because trials with **physically identical** standard and probe stimuli (**0-offset** conditions) would otherwise require a numerical intensity of **0**, a **systematic replacement** was applied: the **0-offset** level was coded as **half of the smallest non-zero stimulus level** tested in each modality—the same **anchor** convention used to generate the descriptive psychometric summaries in @tbl-pf-params. For the **auditory** task, the smallest non-zero **frequency offset** was **8 Hz**, so the **0-offset** condition was assigned **4 Hz**. For the **visual** task, the **0-offset** condition was assigned **0.0075** **Michelson** contrast units. This procedure **retains the full range of difficulty levels** (including the physically identical pair) while ensuring **mathematical compatibility** with the **Psignifit 4** fitting engine.

**Guess and lapse parameters were allowed to vary freely** during fitting (i.e., $\gamma$ and $\lambda$ were free parameters), consistent with psychophysical guidance that fixing lapse at zero can bias threshold and slope estimates when lapses are present [@prins2016psychophysics; @wichmann2001psychometric].

**Threshold and slope (effective midpoint).** Reported **thresholds** and **slopes** were defined at the psychometric function’s **effective midpoint**: the operating point located halfway between the **guess rate** $\gamma$ (lower asymptote) and the **upper asymptote** $1-\lambda$. The response probability at that midpoint is therefore
$$
\text{Threshold} = \gamma + \frac{(1 - \lambda) - \gamma}{2}.
$$
The left-hand side denotes this **midpoint response probability** (on the [0, 1] scale). The **psychometric threshold** values used in subsequent analyses are the **stimulus intensities** $x$ at which the fitted Weibull attains that probability—i.e., the intensity solving $\Psi(x) = \gamma + \frac{(1-\lambda)-\gamma}{2}$ for the fitted psychometric function $\Psi$. **Slope** was evaluated at that same effective midpoint (local steepness of $\Psi$ with respect to stimulus intensity at the threshold stimulus). In substantive terms, this stimulus-level definition indexes the intensity at which the probability of a "different" response is approximately **0.5** on an **effective** scale that adjusts for individual guess and lapse rates—namely, halfway between $\gamma$ and $1-\lambda$ rather than halfway between 0 and 1. This convention yields a criterion comparable to a 50% point on the effective response scale while remaining robust to variation in $\gamma$ and $\lambda$ across participants and conditions.

### Trial-level GLMM (primary model) {#sec-glmm}

The primary model used a probit link function to link phasic arousal to psychometric sensitivity:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{probit}(P(Y_{ij}=1)) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{ij} + \beta_2 \text{Effort}_{ij} + \beta_3 \text{Modality}_{ij} + \beta_4 P^{(\text{state})}_{ij} \\
&\quad + \beta_5 (X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}) + \beta_6 P^{(\text{trait})}_{j} + u_{0j} + u_{1j}X_{ij}
\end{aligned}
$$


where $Y_{ij}$ is the binary choice on trial $i$ for subject $j$, $X_{ij}$ is continuous stimulus intensity, $P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$ is the within-subject centered pupil metric (mean dilation, trial value - subject mean), and $P^{(\text{trait})}_{j}$ is the between-subject pupil metric (subject mean). The key interaction term $X_{ij} \times P^{(\text{state})}_{ij}$ (coefficient $\beta_5$) tests whether within-person fluctuations in arousal are associated with changes in psychometric sensitivity. The term $\beta_6 P^{(\text{trait})}_{j}$ tests whether between-subject differences in average arousal relate to sensitivity, while controlling for state-level effects. The random effects $u_{0j}$ and $u_{1j}$ allow each participant to have their own baseline performance level and intensity sensitivity, respectively.

For model fitting, **stimulus intensity was standardized within task**, and the pupil state and trait components were **z-scored across retained trials** before estimation, so fixed-effect coefficients are interpretable on a standardized latent scale. The probit link was chosen for consistency with signal-detection-style latent evidence formulations; for response probabilities in the present range, probit and logit links would be expected to yield qualitatively similar conclusions. The reported model includes random intercepts and by-subject slopes for stimulus intensity. Exploratory refits that additionally allowed by-subject random slopes for effort and pupil state produced singular fits; those extended specifications were not used for primary inference (see Results).

All GLMMs were estimated using the **lme4** package [@bates2015] in R (version 4.5.3; @R). Models were fit with `glmer` using **lme4** defaults for primary and tiered analyses; the slow-RT sensitivity refit used `glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000))` to stabilize optimization with the reduced trial count. Convergence was assessed by inspecting gradient norms, optimizer warnings, and singular-fit diagnostics. Parameter estimates and standard errors were extracted using the **broom.mixed** package; *p*-values are based on the normal approximation to the *z*-distribution, which is appropriate for large trial-level sample sizes. 95% confidence intervals for fixed effects were computed using the Wald method.

**Robustness, power, and analysis classification.** Trial-level analyses use all available older-adult participants and trials in the LC Aging behavioral–pupil database after preprocessing (see Section 2.1 and Section 3.1); the sample was not sized *de novo* for the continuous-intensity GLMM reported here. The study was designed as a multimodal protocol in which these tasks were embedded alongside imaging and other measures, so the effective *N* reflects recruitment and retention in that broader study rather than a standalone power calculation for the pupil $\times$ intensity interaction. **Prospective** power for that interaction was therefore limited *a priori*. A post-hoc sensitivity power analysis was conducted to estimate the minimum detectable effect size for the primary interaction and realized power from the final sample and design; **numerical results** of that analysis are reported in [@sec-power-analysis](#sec-power-analysis).

Several pre-specified checks supported interpretation of the primary GLMM. **Quality-tier robustness** re-fit the model under `quality_lenient` (more permissive validity: `baseline_quality` and `cog_quality` each $\geq$ 0.50) and `quality_strict` (stricter: each $\geq$ 0.70), in addition to the primary `quality_primary` flag (both $\geq$ 0.60), to assess whether inferences about the stimulus intensity × pupil state interaction depended on inclusion stringency. A **slow-RT subset** restricted analysis to trials with button press after the cognitive window (RT > 1.5 s), to limit motor overlap with the pupil epoch ([@sec-response-timing](#sec-response-timing)). **Model comparison** contrasted the primary model with a nested model omitting the interaction, using Akaike’s information criterion (AIC), where a meaningful improvement (e.g., $\Delta$AIC > 2) would favor retaining the interaction. **Missingness diagnostics** tested whether pupil loss related to effort, intensity, task, or RT (Section 3.4; quality-tier robustness in Section 3.5.1; supplementary tables in **Appendix B**). Finally, **equivalence testing** (two one-sided tests; [@lakens2017]) evaluated the interaction against a pre-specified smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) on the probit scale; the bound rationale is given in [@sec-sesoi-rationale](#sec-sesoi-rationale), and test intervals and outcome are summarized in [@sec-pupil-quality-tier](#sec-pupil-quality-tier).

The prospectus-defined **confirmatory** targets were effort effects on psychometric parameters (RQ1), the effort–pupil manipulation check (RQ2), trial-level pupil–psychometric coupling (RQ3), and subject-level PF–pupil coupling (RQ4). **Pre-specified sensitivity analyses** (quality tiers, model comparison, slow-RT subset, equivalence) were used to stress-test those inferences, not to add new hypotheses. **Exploratory** analyses would have been any post-hoc tests outside the prospectus; none were run beyond what is reported, and all reported statistics correspond to the pre-registered plan.

# Results

Results below follow the pre-registered pipeline: psychometric parameters, effort–pupil manipulation checks, missingness, trial-level coupling, subject-level coupling, and a hypothesis summary. Unless noted otherwise, models use the primary pupil-quality tier (baseline and cognitive window validity $\geq$ 0.60).

## Data Quality and Sample Sizes

```{r tbl-sample-flow}

PF = psychometric threshold greater than 64 Hz (Psignifit validity criteria for the auditory stimulus range); QC = excessive eye-track loss (greater than 50% invalid samples) or other pupil quality-control failure."

    format(nt_adt_q, big.mark = ","), " ADT trials and ",
    format(nt_vdt_q, big.mark = ","), " VDT trials (",
    format(nt_total_q, big.mark = ","), " total) met the quality gate. ",
    "The primary GLMM further required non-missing cognitive pupil state, stimulus intensity, and choice, ",
    "yielding ", format(glmm_primary_sample$n_trials, big.mark = ","),
    " complete-case trials from ", glmm_primary_sample$n_sub,
    " participants (mean ", sprintf("%.1f", glmm_primary_sample$mean_trials_per_sub),
    " trials per participant). Post-hoc power (@sec-power-analysis) uses this GLMM sample, ",
    "not the full quality-primary trial count.\n\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("*Primary-tier and GLMM sample counts could not be computed (merged data unavailable in this render). Final N is fixed in @tbl-sample-flow.*\n\n")
}
```

## Behavioral Backbone (PF Outcomes)

```{r pf-backbone}
#| label: tbl-pf-params
#| tbl-cap: "Psychometric Function Parameters by Task and Effort (descriptive means and SDs)"

if (!is.null(pf_params)) {
  pf_summary <- filter_pf_analysis(pf_params) %>%
    group_by(task, effort) %>%
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      threshold_mean = mean(threshold, na.rm = TRUE),
      threshold_sd = sd(threshold, na.rm = TRUE),
      slope_mean = mean(slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      slope_sd = sd(slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  pf_summary %>%
    make_table(
      col.names = c("Task", "Effort", "N", "Threshold (M)", "Threshold (SD)", 
                   "Slope (M)", "Slope (SD)"),
      digits = 3
    )
} else {
  cat("*PF parameters not yet computed.*")
}
```

Psychometric function parameters for each modality and effort condition are summarized in @tbl-pf-params (PF-valid sample; @sec-analytic-samples).

```{r tbl-pf-effort-test}
#| label: tbl-pf-effort-test
#| tbl-cap: "Within-Subject Tests of Effort on PF Threshold and Slope (High − Low). PF-valid sample: converged fits; ADT thresholds ≤ 64 Hz."

library(lme4)

if (!is.null(pf_params)) {
  pf_h1_infer <- bind_rows(
    lapply(c("ADT", "VDT"), function(tsk) {
      bind_rows(
        lapply(c("threshold", "slope"), function(out) {
          extract_pf_effort_lmer(pf_params, tsk, out)
        })
      )
    })
  )
  if (nrow(pf_h1_infer) > 0) {
    pf_h1_infer %>%
      mutate(
        `Est. (High − Low)` = round(`Est. (High − Low)`, 3),
        SE = round(SE, 3),
        t = round(t, 3),
        df = round(df, 2),
        p = round(p, 4),
        N = n_sub
      ) %>%
      select(-n_sub) %>%
      make_table(
        col.names = c(
          "Task", "PF Parameter", "Est. (High − Low)", "SE", "t", "df", "p", "N"
        ),
        digits = 3
      )
  } else {
    cat("*Could not fit PF effort models (insufficient data).*")
    pf_h1_infer <- tibble()
  }
} else {
  cat("*PF parameters not available for inferential tests.*")
  pf_h1_infer <- tibble()
}
```

```{r pf-h1-interpret, results = "asis"}
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  if (is.na(p)) {
    return("—")
  }
  if (p < 0.001) {
    return("< .001")
  }
  sprintf("%.3f", p)
}

if (!is.null(pf_h1_infer) && nrow(pf_h1_infer) == 4) {
  getr <- function(tsk, par) {
    pf_h1_infer %>% dplyr::filter(Task == tsk, `PF Parameter` == par) %>% dplyr::slice(1)
  }
  adt_th <- getr("ADT", "Threshold")
  adt_sl <- getr("ADT", "Slope")
  vdt_th <- getr("VDT", "Threshold")
  vdt_sl <- getr("VDT", "Slope")

  cat(
    "@tbl-pf-effort-test summarizes within-subject High vs. Low effort contrasts on threshold and slope. **Auditory (ADT).** Threshold increased under High effort (estimate = ",
    adt_th$`Est. (High − Low)`,
    ", *t*(",
    round(adt_th$df, 1),
    ") = ",
    round(adt_th$t, 3),
    ", *p* = ",
    fmt_p(adt_th$p),
    "), consistent with H1a. Slope was slightly lower under High effort (estimate = ",
    adt_sl$`Est. (High − Low)`,
    ", *t*(",
    round(adt_sl$df, 1),
    ") = ",
    round(adt_sl$t, 3),
    ", *p* = ",
    fmt_p(adt_sl$p),
    "); the shallowing predicted by H1b was in the expected direction but not statistically reliable. **Visual (VDT).** Threshold did not differ reliably between effort conditions (estimate = ",
    vdt_th$`Est. (High − Low)`,
    ", *t*(",
    round(vdt_th$df, 1),
    ") = ",
    round(vdt_th$t, 3),
    ", *p* = ",
    fmt_p(vdt_th$p),
    "). Slopes were lower under High effort (estimate = ",
    vdt_sl$`Est. (High − Low)`,
    ", *t*(",
    round(vdt_sl$df, 1),
    ") = ",
    round(vdt_sl$t, 3),
    ", *p* = ",
    fmt_p(vdt_sl$p),
    "), again matching the direction of H1b without statistical support at conventional levels.\n\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("*Inferential tests for PF effort effects not available.*\n\n")
}
```

```{r pf-adt-slope-variance-interpretation}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis

fmt_p_line <- function(p) {
  if (length(p) == 0L) {
    return("—")
  }
  p <- p[[1]]
  if (is.na(p)) {
    return("—")
  }
  if (p < 0.001) {
    return("< .001")
  }
  sprintf("%.3f", p)
}

if (!is.null(pf_params)) {
  adt <- filter_pf_analysis(pf_params) %>% dplyr::filter(task == "ADT")
  m_pooled <- mean(adt$slope, na.rm = TRUE)
  sd_pooled <- stats::sd(adt$slope)
  adt_by_eff <- filter_pf_analysis(pf_params) %>%
    dplyr::filter(task == "ADT", effort %in% c("Low", "High")) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(effort) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      slope_m = mean(slope, na.rm = TRUE),
      slope_sd = stats::sd(slope),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  low_m <- adt_by_eff %>% dplyr::filter(effort == "Low") %>% dplyr::pull(slope_m)
  high_m <- adt_by_eff %>% dplyr::filter(effort == "High") %>% dplyr::pull(slope_m)
  low_sd <- adt_by_eff %>% dplyr::filter(effort == "Low") %>% dplyr::pull(slope_sd)
  high_sd <- adt_by_eff %>% dplyr::filter(effort == "High") %>% dplyr::pull(slope_sd)
  low_m <- if (length(low_m)) low_m[[1]] else NA_real_
  high_m <- if (length(high_m)) high_m[[1]] else NA_real_
  low_sd <- if (length(low_sd)) low_sd[[1]] else NA_real_
  high_sd <- if (length(high_sd)) high_sd[[1]] else NA_real_
  adt_p <- NA_real_
  vdt_p <- NA_real_
  if (exists("pf_h1_infer") && !is.null(pf_h1_infer) && nrow(pf_h1_infer) > 0) {
    r1 <- pf_h1_infer %>% dplyr::filter(Task == "ADT", `PF Parameter` == "Slope")
    r2 <- pf_h1_infer %>% dplyr::filter(Task == "VDT", `PF Parameter` == "Slope")
    if (nrow(r1) > 0) adt_p <- r1$p[1]
    if (nrow(r2) > 0) vdt_p <- r2$p[1]
  }
  cat(
    "**Auditory slope variance (high-precision PF estimates).** ",
    "Descriptive slopes in @tbl-pf-params are based on full-precision Psignifit parameters (no rounding-induced compression). ",
    "For **ADT**, participant-level slopes showed **healthy, biologically plausible** spread: ",
    "pooled across effort conditions, **M** = **", sprintf("%.3f", m_pooled), "**, **SD** = **", sprintf("%.3f", sd_pooled), "**; ",
    "by condition, means were **", sprintf("%.3f", low_m), "** (Low) and **", sprintf("%.3f", high_m), "** (High), ",
    "with SDs **", sprintf("%.3f", low_sd), "** and **", sprintf("%.3f", high_sd), "**, matching @tbl-pf-params. ",
    "Despite this informative between-person variance, the within-subject effort contrast on **slope** was **not significant** for **ADT** (*p* = ", fmt_p_line(adt_p), ") or **VDT** (*p* = ", fmt_p_line(vdt_p), "; @tbl-pf-effort-test). ",
    "Together with the **null** slope effects in **both** modalities, this pattern supports treating the grip manipulation as a **physiological stressor** that **did not** reliably impair **perceptual** discrimination slopes—arguing against a simple confound of effort with psychometric sensitivity at the PF level.\n\n",
    sep = ""
  )
} else {
  cat("")
}
```

**Hypothesis Testing (H1a & H1b):** Hypothesis 1a predicted higher midpoint thresholds under High effort. This pattern received **partial support**: the increase was **statistically significant for ADT** (*p* &lt; .05) but **not for VDT**. Because multiple confirmatory tests were evaluated across H1/H2, this isolated ADT threshold effect should be treated as fragile rather than definitive on its own. Hypothesis 1b predicted shallower PF slopes under High effort; **slopes were numerically shallower** (negative High − Low estimates) in **both** modalities, but **neither** slope contrast reached significance (@tbl-pf-effort-test). Thus H1b was **not supported** as a confirmatory inference. The **cross-modal** consistency of the slope null (see paragraph above) reinforces that the behavioral pattern is **not** specific to a single modality or to artifactually compressed auditory parameters.

## Effort–Pupil Manipulation Check

@fig-pupil-timeseries shows **empirical** group-mean pupil waveforms from the preprocessing pipeline: baseline-corrected isolated pupil (arbitrary units) with GAM-smoothed 95% CI bands (winsorized subject-level means), time-locked to squeeze onset, separately for ADT and VDT. Lines correspond to the factorial combination of stimulus difficulty (Easy vs. Hard) and handgrip effort (High vs. Low). Vertical markers indicate squeeze onset, standard and target onsets, and median response time (task-specific subtitles). Horizontal bars mark the pre-trial baseline (B0), the Total AUC window (0--4.70 s), the pre-stimulus baseline (B1), and the cognitive AUC window (4.85--6.05 s). These plots are observed data rather than the parametric schematic used in earlier drafts.

```{r pupil-timeseries-fig}
#| label: fig-pupil-timeseries
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Full-trial pupil waveforms (empirical group means). Baseline-corrected isolated pupil diameter
#|   (arbitrary units; GAM 95% CI on winsorized subject means) as a function of time relative to squeeze onset,
#|   for ADT (top) and VDT (bottom).
#|   Colored lines cross Easy vs. Hard stimulus difficulty with High vs. Low grip effort.
#|   Vertical dashed lines mark squeeze onset, standard (S1) and target (S2/probe) onsets, and median response onset.
#|   Grey and colored bars show B0, Total AUC (0--4.70 s), B1, and cognitive AUC (4.85--6.05 s).
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

waveform_path <- file.path(chapter2_dir, "output", "figures", "waveform.png")
if (file.exists(waveform_path)) {
  knitr::include_graphics(waveform_path)
} else {
  cat("*Figure: waveform.png not found. Expected at:* ", waveform_path, "*")
}
```

As predicted, high-effort handgrip significantly increased overall trial-period arousal (Total AUC: $\beta = 0.857$, $SE = 0.376$, $t = 2.282$, $p = .023$), but significantly attenuated task-evoked responses (Cognitive AUC: $\beta = -0.012$, $SE = 0.003$, $t = -3.859$, $p < .001$). Total AUC indexes overall arousal during the sustained squeeze epoch; Cognitive AUC is the stimulus-locked task-evoked response in the discrimination window. This dissociation is consistent with attenuated task-evoked phasic responding under concurrent high effort, but it is not uniquely diagnostic of such suppression: because the cognitive metric is baseline-corrected subtractively, a higher pre-target baseline under High effort could also reduce the apparent dynamic range available for subsequent dilation. A simple physiological-ceiling account — whereby High-effort trials would cluster at the upper extreme of the observed Cognitive AUC distribution — was not supported: High-effort trials were not disproportionately concentrated in the upper tail relative to Low-effort trials, which is inconsistent with a hard iris ceiling and instead favors interpreting the pattern in terms of reduced dynamic range after baseline elevation. Mixed-effects models tested whether effort condition predicted pupil metrics (Total AUC and Cognitive AUC) while controlling for task modality.

**Note:** Hypothesis 2a (tonic arousal) was operationalized using Total AUC — the baseline-corrected area under the pupil curve over the global trial window — rather than a dedicated pre-stimulus baseline pupil measure. Total AUC during the squeeze epoch captures sustained arousal-related dilation that reflects both tonic state and the ongoing effort response, making it an appropriate but imperfect proxy for tonic arousal. A pre-stimulus baseline measure would more directly index tonic pupil state and could be explored in future analyses.

**Hypothesis Testing:** Hypothesis 2a predicted that tonic arousal would be elevated under High effort; this received **indirect, qualified support** via the significant increase in Total AUC (statistics above), recognizing that Total AUC is not a pure tonic measure. Hypothesis 2b predicted that task-evoked pupil responses (Cognitive AUC) would also be larger under High effort; this hypothesis was not supported — instead, Cognitive AUC was significantly *reduced* under High effort (statistics above). Rather than confirming a uniform arousal increase, these results suggest a tonic-phasic dissociation whose interpretation remains non-exclusive: the pattern is compatible with phasic suppression or reallocation under high effort, but could also partly reflect reduced dynamic range after baseline elevation.

## Missingness Diagnostic

Missingness was significantly predicted by effort condition (OR = 1.203, *z* = 3.672, *p* < .001) and task modality (OR = 1.967, *z* = 12.584, *p* < .001), but not by stimulus intensity (*p* = .565) or response time (*p* = .982). High-effort trials were approximately 20% more likely to yield usable pupil data than Low-effort trials, possibly reflecting reduced blinking during the more demanding squeeze. VDT trials had nearly twice the odds of retaining usable data relative to ADT trials. Crucially, missingness is not predicted by stimulus intensity or response time, suggesting that within-retained trials the psychometric intensity range and decision difficulty are not systematically distorted. Nevertheless, the non-random missingness by effort and task means that analysis samples differ systematically across conditions, which is a genuine selection-bias limitation (see [@sec-missingness-limitation](#sec-missingness-limitation)). Full model output and the RT-by-availability figure are in [Appendix C](#sec-appendix-c).

## Pupil–Psychometric Coupling (Primary Analysis)

```{r primary-coupling}
#| label: tbl-pupil-psychometric
#| tbl-cap: "Primary GLMM: Pupil–Psychometric Coupling"

if (!is.null(pupil_psychometric_effects)) {
  library(lme4)
  tbl <- pupil_psychometric_effects %>%
    dplyr::select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value)

  mod_primary_path <- file.path(models_dir, "mod_pupil_psychometric_primary.rds")
  if (file.exists(mod_primary_path)) {
    mod_primary <- readRDS(mod_primary_path)
    ci_wald <- confint(mod_primary, method = "Wald", parm = "beta_")
    ci_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
      term = rownames(ci_wald),
      `95% CI Lower` = ci_wald[, 1L],
      `95% CI Upper` = ci_wald[, 2L]
    )
    tbl <- dplyr::left_join(tbl, ci_tbl, by = "term")
  } else {
    tbl <- tbl %>%
      dplyr::mutate(
        `95% CI Lower` = estimate - stats::qnorm(0.975) * std.error,
        `95% CI Upper` = estimate + stats::qnorm(0.975) * std.error
      )
  }

  term_labels <- c(
    "(Intercept)"                                              = "Intercept",
    "stimulus_intensity_scaled"                                = "Stimulus Intensity",
    "pupil_cognitive_state_scaled"                             = "Cognitive Pupil State (within-person)",
    "effort_factorHigh"                                        = "Effort: High vs. Low",
    "task_factorVDT"                                           = "Task: VDT vs. ADT",
    "pupil_cognitive_trait_scaled"                             = "Cognitive Pupil Trait (between-person)",
    "stimulus_intensity_scaled:pupil_cognitive_state_scaled"   = "Stimulus Intensity × Pupil State",
    "rt_scaled"                                                = "Reaction Time (covariate)"
  )

  tbl <- tbl %>%
    dplyr::mutate(term = dplyr::recode(term, !!!term_labels)) %>%
    dplyr::select(term, estimate, `95% CI Lower`, `95% CI Upper`, std.error, statistic, p.value)

  make_table(
    tbl,
    col.names = c("Term", "Estimate", "95% CI Lower", "95% CI Upper", "SE", "z", "p"),
    digits = 4
  )
} else {
  cat("*Primary coupling analysis results not yet available.*")
}
```

**Hypothesis Testing:** Hypothesis 3a predicted a negative interaction between stimulus intensity and pupil state, consistent with supra-optimal arousal degrading sensitivity and producing shallower psychometric slopes on high-arousal trials. **The interaction between stimulus intensity and pupil state was not significant** ($\beta = 0.035$, $p = .245$; @tbl-pupil-psychometric). The point estimate was in the **opposite direction** to Hypothesis 3a ($\mathrm{SE} = 0.030$, 95% Wald CI $[-0.024,\, +0.095]$; $z = 1.163$): higher trial-level arousal was associated with marginally steeper (not shallower) slopes, which, if real, would align with the alternative Hypothesis 3b (moderate arousal enhancing sensitivity). The interval is wide enough to include small negative effects, near-null effects, and modest positive effects, which is informative about the precision of the null finding. The negative effort main effect ($\beta = -0.139$, $z = -3.023$, $p = .003$) indicates that High effort reduced overall probability of "different" responding, which is more appropriately described as an intercept or response-tendency shift than as a demonstrated signal-detection-theoretic criterion shift. Pupil state as a main effect approached but did not reach significance ($\beta = -0.046$, $z = -1.912$, $p = .056$), suggesting a marginal tendency for higher arousal to be associated with reduced overall responding. The pupil trait main effect was not significant ($\beta = -0.052$, $z = -0.575$, $p = .565$), consistent with Hypothesis 3c.

**Interpretation of Results:** At the primary quality tier, the stimulus intensity $\times$ pupil state interaction was **non-significant** ($p = .245$), and the point estimate was **positive**—opposite to Hypothesis 3a. Plausible accounts include limited power, mismatch between the fixed cognitive pupil window and arousal dynamics most relevant to choice, or a weak or null true coupling; pre-specified sensitivity analyses (below and [Appendix B](#sec-appendix-b)) qualify this pattern.

Model-predicted psychometric functions at low (−1 SD) and high (+1 SD) pupil state are shown in [Appendix B](#sec-appendix-b) (@fig-appendix-b1-predicted); the apparent visual separation of curves reflects extrapolation across the full scaled intensity range and should not be interpreted as evidence of a reliable effect given that the interaction was **not significant** ($\beta = 0.035$, 95% CI $[-0.024,\, +0.095]$, $p = .245$).

if (!is.null(fig_path_abs) && file.exists(fig_path_abs)) {

  if (!is.null(fig_path_abs2) && file.exists(fig_path_abs2)) {
